posts.title: A percentage cut costs most in your best month
posts.body:
A form tool that takes a percentage of your payments earns the most from you in your best month.

A percentage cut grows with every sale. Each extra booking adds to it, and a large project deposit makes it larger. It's easy to miss, because it comes out of each payment instead of arriving as a bill you'd notice and question.

That matters most when the form is how you get paid. A freelancer taking a booking deposit. A studio that needs payment before a project starts. An organiser selling places on a workshop. For all of them, the cost rises exactly when the form is doing its job.

So we built Formkit the other way round. Payments go straight into your own Stripe account and we take no cut. What you pay us is flat: Pro is $6 a seat a month, with two months free if you pay yearly. A good month for you doesn't change our price.

Before you pick any tool to take payments through a form, ask two questions. Does the money land in my own account? Does the tool take a share of each payment on top of what the payment processor charges? Those two answers tell you what the form really costs once it starts working.

How do you take deposits today: an invoice after the call, or a payment inside the form?

posts.title: Stop writing the same form twice
posts.body:
Drafting a form in ChatGPT, then rebuilding it field by field in a builder, is the same job done twice.

The draft in the chat is usually the better thinking. It's the conversation where you worked out who fills the form in, what you need from them and what you'll do with each answer. Retyping it into a separate tool adds nothing, except a chance to drop or change a question on the way.

So Formkit works inside Claude and ChatGPT: you build and publish the form in the same conversation where you planned it. It works on every plan, including the free one, which has unlimited forms, responses and members.

The catch is that the form is only as good as the description you give the assistant. Say who will fill it in, which answers are required, and what decision each answer feeds. A question that doesn't change what you do next probably doesn't belong on the form.

The document below shows how to write that description, using a client intake form as the example.

Would you let an assistant publish a form without opening it in a builder first? If not, what's the first thing you'd check?

posts.title: Find the question where people quit
posts.body:
Your form only shows you the people who finished it. The ones who quit halfway leave no trace.

That hides the most useful thing a form can tell you: which question made people stop. When an enquiry form gets fewer replies than you expected, the usual instinct is to cut questions at random or rewrite the whole thing. Both are guesses.

The better move is to measure, question by question, how many people reached each one and how many carried on. The biggest gap between two questions points at the one to change. Candidates worth checking first: a budget question asked before you've explained anything, a required phone number, a file upload that's awkward to do on a phone.

Formkit shows drop-off by question and keeps partial responses on every plan, including the free one. So you change that one question, leave the rest alone, and see whether the drop at that point shrinks.

If you have a form live right now, pick the question you'd bet loses the most people. Then check whether your current tool can prove it.

Which question on your forms do people quit at most?

output.positioning: Frame: the free form builder with no response cap, aimed at Typeform switchers. Building in Claude or ChatGPT is the wedge. Style: big fish, small pond. • Frames compared: (1) 'Typeform alternative': obvious value for switchers and sets a lower-price expectation that $6 a seat fits. But it invites a design fight Typeform wins in reviews, so use it as a keyword, not an identity. (2) 'Free form builder with no response cap': instantly clear, matches the top complaint (price or caps in 11 of 18 snippets) and sets a $0 expectation that Free meets. Risk: Tally also offers free unlimited submissions. (3) 'Form builder in ChatGPT and Claude': the most distinct, but search demand is unknown, it needs explaining and it sets no price expectation. Chosen: (2), with (3) as proof it isn't just another free tool. • Rejected: head-to-head with Typeform, because its interface is praised and Formkit has zero reviews to prove parity. Also rejected: a new category such as 'AI form agent', because a $600 monthly budget can't educate a market. • Swap test: Typeform and Fillout fail on uncapped free responses. Tally fails on in-chat building, if its MCP status checks out as absent. • Headlines: 'Unlimited forms and responses, on the free plan.' / 'Overpaying for your form builder? Start free with unlimited responses.' / 'Build and publish forms without leaving Claude or ChatGPT.' • Subheads: 'No response cap on Free. Move to Pro at $6 a seat when you want your own domain.' / 'See the question people quit on, and keep their half-finished answers, on the free plan.' / 'Take payments through your own Stripe account. The money goes straight to you, and Formkit takes no cut.' • Pillar 1, no cap: Free includes unlimited forms, responses and members. Contrast: Typeform's free plan allows 10 responses a month (third-party source; verify and date it before use). • Pillar 2, build where you already work: Claude and ChatGPT can build and publish Formkit forms. • Pillar 3, pricing that stays fair: Pro is $6 a seat, yearly billing gives two months free, Stripe payments carry no Formkit cut, and cancelling takes one click with no survey. • Words to use: overpaying, a fraction of the price, a decent number of responses, capped, limits, clunky, look professional, test run. • Words to avoid: AI-powered, unlimited AI (Pro AI replies cover 20 responses a seat), seamless, solutions, best, 'only Formkit' (MCP is unverified for rivals), free custom domain. • Landing page order: 1 headline and 'Start free'; 2 the problem in customer words (caps, overpaying); 3 the alternatives and their trade-offs (Typeform caps, Tally's paid domain); 4 what to look for (no cap, drop-off data, payments with no cut); 5 the three pillars with proof; 6 pricing at $0, $6 and $19 a seat, yearly two months free; 7 FAQ (domain on Pro, one-click cancel); 8 'Build a form' CTA.
output.pricingNotes: Formkit Pro is $6 a seat a month ($5 billed yearly). Business is $19 a seat. Free is $0. • At 1 seat: Formkit Pro $6, Fillout Starter $15 (annual), Tally Pro about $29, Typeform from $39 monthly. All rival prices are third-party, undated and unverified. • Per-seat pricing erodes the advantage as teams grow. On yearly billing, 3 Pro seats cost $15 ($5 × 3), the same as Fillout Starter. On monthly billing, 5 Pro seats cost $30 ($6 × 5), more than Tally's roughly $29. Tally's and Fillout's seat models were not confirmed. • Pro AI replies cover 20 responses a seat a month; credits start at $5 for 100. Never advertise 'unlimited AI'. • Custom domains are Pro-only, as on Tally. That is parity, not a differentiator. • Stripe payments carry no Formkit cut. Rivals' fees were not checked, so make no contrast claim.

opportunities.title: 3-week Google Search test on switcher intent
opportunities.why: Week 1 (days 1–7): launch 3 ad groups, 'typeform alternative', 'free form builder unlimited responses' and 'form builder chatgpt claude', splitting the $600 monthly budget evenly (assumption: $200 each). Week 2 (days 8–14): judge each group only after 100 clicks. The primary metric is sign-up rate; the secondary is paid upgrades per $100. Pause any group whose sign-up rate is under half the best group's. Week 3 (days 15–21): move its budget to the best group. Read results as directional because volume is low.

output.positioningStatement: For freelancers and small teams of 1–3 seats who pay for Typeform or keep hitting a free plan's response cap, Formkit is the free form builder with no response cap. Unlike Typeform's free plan (10 responses a month, per a third-party source), Formkit Free has unlimited forms, responses and members, and you can build and publish forms from Claude or ChatGPT. Pro is $6 a seat when you want your own domain, and Stripe payments go straight to you with no Formkit cut.
output.confidenceNotes: • Thin bank: 18 verbatim snippets, all from competitors' customers: Typeform 8 (Capterra), Tally 7 (Trustpilot, G2, hackceleration), Jotform 3 (Capterra). Own-customer snippets: 0. • Finding, price: 8 of 18 snippets (Typeform 5 of 8; Tally 2 of 7; Jotform 1 of 3) from 6 pages on 2 platforms. • Finding, free-plan caps and limits: 5 of 18 snippets (Typeform 3, Jotform 1, Tally 1) on 2 platforms. Price or caps combined: 11 of 18. • Signals only: domain or Pro limits (2), looks (2), design bar (2), complexity (1). • Competitor prices are third-party, undated and vary by source. • Not accessed: rival homepages, ad libraries, Reddit. • Confidence: segment Medium; frame Medium; in-chat angle Low. Validate with the 3-week search test and 5 calls asking 'what did you use before?'

v22.topIssue: The chosen frame, 'free form builder with no response cap', is matched by Tally's free unlimited submissions, and the swot itself admits this. The only real differentiator is the in-chat building angle, rated low confidence. The positioning therefore rests on a claim the closest rival can equal, and on internal figures (20 AI replies a seat, $5 credits, 30-day version history) that don't trace to the confirmed facts.

output.summary: Sell Pro at the moment free users need it, not through ads. Primary: an upgrade screen when a free user clicks a Pro-only feature. Secondary: cold email to small agencies. Hygiene: a one-off, capped Claude directory listing. Ad spend stays at $0 unless the wall proves too small at the start of week 3. Monthly Pro at $6 cannot fund paid traffic, so any paid traffic leads with yearly Pro or Business.
output.positioning: Formkit is the form builder for when the form is part of how people see you. Describe a form and AI builds it, even inside Claude or ChatGPT. Pro puts it on your own domain with no badge and sends payments to your own Stripe account, with no cut taken. Every channel leads with 'no cut on payments' and 'looks like yours', not 'free', because Tally and Google Forms are free too.

output.portfolioNote:
Lead with the upgrade moment, not ads. One Pro seat is worth about $58 gross profit in its first year ($6 × 12 months × an assumed 80% margin; assumption, grade D), so most paid channels cannot pay back.
- **Play 1, bankable (score 90/100):** upgrade free users when they hit a Pro-only feature.
- **Play 2, creative (70/100):** win agencies with chat-built client forms in per-client workspaces.
- **Play 3, moonshot (70/100):** list Formkit in the Claude directory. Distinctiveness is 4, not 5, because Typeform, Jotform, Cognito Forms and FormHug already work with Claude. Formkit's edge is that it works on the free plan.
- **Ad test:** put one fifth of the $600 monthly budget into Google search for 'google forms alternative' and 'tally alternative'. Send clicks to a Google Forms switcher page built from Formkit's compare table.
  - Add negative keywords vue, react, npm and github. FormKit, the Vue library at formkit.com, shares the name.
  - Kill after one month if each new Pro account costs more than $58. Widen to half the budget if it costs under half that and brings at least 3 Pro accounts.
  - Click costs were not checked in this research.
- **Skipped:** Product Hunt (assumption: tens of owner hours for mostly free signups) and paid newsletters (no click-cost data in this research).
